questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A default that widens reach
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a permissive default enlarges the reachable surface of a system
questions.stem: A depot console trusts any device that can reach its port, without checking who the device is. What does that default widen?

options.text: The set of devices that can reach and use the console without proving who they are
options.misconception: thinks trust only affects the operator's own screen

options.text: Only the number of console screens inside the depot building, nothing beyond it
options.misconception: believes reach stops at the walls of one depot

options.text: The response time of the depot radio channel when traffic is heavy
options.misconception: confuses reach with the speed of another system

options.text: The number of timetable stops the console is configured to display
options.misconception: maps a technical setting onto the service schedule

questions.explanation: A permissive default lets any reachable device inherit the console capabilities, so reach grows without any change to the device count. Treating trust as a display concern instead of a reach concern is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask who can now use the console.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness that lives in the settings
questions.learningObjective: Interpret overlapping weakness counts without assuming the groups are the same
questions.stem: A review found 14 consoles with permissive default trust and 9 with an exposed management page, and 6 consoles appear in both lists. What does this support?

options.text: Every exposed console also trusts any device, so the two weaknesses always travel together
options.misconception: assumes the two lists describe identical sets

options.text: Six consoles carry both weaknesses, so fixing defaults alone still leaves an exposed page
options.misconception: ignores the overlap between the two lists

options.text: Only the four consoles on neither list need follow-up work in the following week
options.misconception: treats absence from both lists as permission to ignore

options.text: The nine exposed consoles outnumber the fourteen default-trust consoles in every respect
options.misconception: compares two totals without checking the overlap

questions.explanation: Because six consoles sit in both lists, the weaknesses overlap but do not coincide, so the groups cannot be treated as one set. Assuming the lists match is the tempting error, and it hides consoles with only one weakness.
questions.hint: Check whether the lists share members.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness with no fix to install
questions.learningObjective: Calculate residual exposure after mitigation steps when no patch exists
questions.stem: A depot console exposes 240 operator accounts. A mitigation closes access for 60 percent of them, then a second change closes 20 more of the survivors. How many accounts still work?
questions.explanation: Closing 60 percent of 240 leaves 96 accounts reachable. The second change removes 20 of those, leaving 76 exposed accounts, which is the residual reach once both mitigations are in place.
questions.hint: Apply the percentage first, then subtract.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The interval between disclosure and deployment
questions.learningObjective: Relate the time between disclosure and deployment to the exposure window
questions.stem: Across the network, an advisory went out on Tuesday and the patched image lands in eleven days. How should the planner describe the interval?

options.text: A closed window, because the advisory already tells operators what to avoid
options.misconception: believes publishing an advisory applies the fix

options.text: An eleven-day window in which the weakness remains usable until the patch is running
options.misconception: counts the window as ending at publication time

options.text: A window of one day, since Tuesday and the next Tuesday are one day apart
options.misconception: miscounts the gap between two Tuesdays

options.text: No window at all, because weaknesses do not exist until a build is shipped
options.misconception: believes a weakness only exists once a fix appears

questions.explanation: The gap between an advisory and the running patch is exactly the period in which the weakness can still be used. Treating publication as the end of the window, or miscounting the days, is the tempting error in this area.
questions.hint: Count days from the advisory to the running patch.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of handling a published weakness
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for handling a published weakness correctly
questions.stem: Explain in order why a transit planner checks whether a published weakness applies to the depot before attempting any temporary workaround.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that an advisory describes a weakness in general, so the planner must first confirm that the depot's own version and configuration expose it; a weakness that does not apply here should not consume effort or cause pointless disruption. Only once applicability is established does ordering by exposure decide what is fixed first, and any temporary workaround follows that judgement rather than replacing it.

questions.explanation: The advisory is general, so applicability to the depot must come first; ordering by exposure only makes sense over weaknesses that are actually present here. Attempting a workaround before checking applicability risks disrupting service for no benefit.
questions.hint: Applicability has to be settled before priorities or workarounds.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Ranking groups by exposure rather than by count
questions.learningObjective: Rank weaknesses by exposure instead of by raw number of affected items

stimulus.body: The advisory describes three weaknesses. One affects ninety depot terminals but only on a segment isolated from the public network. A second affects twelve terminals that bridge onto the public network. A third affects forty terminals on an internal segment with no onward path.

questions.stem: Given that note, which weakness should the planner remediate first?

options.text: The one affecting ninety terminals, because the largest group deserves the earliest slot
options.misconception: ranks by number of items and ignores the onward path

options.text: The one affecting forty terminals, because it sits on an internal segment already
options.misconception: assumes an internal segment means the weakness is harmless

options.text: The one affecting twelve terminals, because it bridges onto the public network
options.misconception: picks the smallest count without checking its path out

options.text: All three together, since a published advisory should be worked as a single block
options.misconception: treats one advisory as one indivisible unit of work

questions.explanation: Exposure depends on whether the affected items can be reached onward, and the twelve bridging terminals offer a path from outside. Ranking purely by count is the tempting error, because ninety on an isolated segment is less reachable than twelve that connect outward.
questions.hint: Ask which affected items can be reached from outside.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Rating against reach
questions.learningObjective: Weigh reach evidence when judging whether two weakness ratings are consistent
questions.stem: Two routes share one weakness. One reaches it through a hardened bastion, the other through an unmanaged phone on the same wireless. How does reach shape the rating?

options.text: The route through the unmanaged phone rates higher, because its path in is shorter
options.misconception: assumes reach depends only on the number of hops

options.text: Both routes rate the same, since the weakness itself is identical in both cases
options.misconception: ignores path differences and rates the weakness alone

options.text: The route through the bastion rates higher, because it is a deliberate piece of infrastructure
options.misconception: believes named infrastructure always raises the risk

options.text: Neither route can be rated until someone counts the devices on each side
options.misconception: believes device counts are the only input to a rating

questions.explanation: The same weakness carries a different rating depending on how easily an attacker can reach it, and an unmanaged phone on the same wireless is a shorter path than a hardened bastion. Rating the weakness in isolation, ignoring the path, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Same weakness, different paths, different reach.

questions.stem: Every console in the yard ships with a guest account that needs no password. What does that default allow?

options.text: Only a printed list of the guest accounts in use at the depot
options.misconception: thinks a guest account is a record of past logins

options.text: A single shared password that the shift supervisor changes each morning
options.misconception: assumes guest access still requires a managed credential

options.text: Anyone at the console without credentials, which widens who can reach it
options.misconception: believes the guest account is limited to depot staff

options.text: A faster login for the depot's own trained dispatchers
options.misconception: treats guest access as a convenience for known staff

questions.explanation: A guest account with no credential lets any device at the console act on it, so the reachable set grows to include whoever is nearest. Believing guest access is limited to trained depot staff is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Count who can act without proving who they are.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness that lives in the settings
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a weakness that arises purely from a configuration value
questions.stem: Within the depot, one console lets operators switch off the session timeout from the same panel that shows the timetable. Why is that a settings weakness?

options.text: The timeout is a setting the operator can weaken at run time, so it fails open on demand
options.misconception: blames the panel layout rather than the value it exposes

options.text: The timetable display is too large for the console, so the timeout cannot be read
options.misconception: treats a display size limit as a configuration fault

options.text: Operators dislike the timeout, so the weakness is really a training issue
options.misconception: reframes a technical weakness as a matter of preference

options.text: Nothing in the settings is wrong, since timeouts are optional by design
options.misconception: treats a design choice as automatically harmless

questions.explanation: The weakness lives in a value the operator can change from a live panel, which means protection can be removed at run time without any vendor update. Calling it a training issue or a display problem is the tempting error, since neither addresses the exposed control.
questions.hint: Ask who can change that value while the system runs.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness with no fix to install
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a weakness without a vendor fix can still be reduced
questions.stem: Every console at four depots shares a weakness that no vendor build can repair, and several responses have been considered. Which conclusion does the evidence support?

options.text: No progress is possible until a vendor build appears, so the depots must simply wait
options.misconception: believes exposure is fixed only by a vendor patch

options.text: The depots must isolate all consoles from every network, including the internal one
options.misconception: jumps straight to total isolation with no middle step

options.text: The weakness is only theoretical because the vendor has not confirmed it yet
options.misconception: treats unconfirmed status as proof of safety

options.text: Exposure can still be reduced by retiring the feature or limiting who can reach it
options.misconception: thinks removal of a feature counts as destroying data

questions.explanation: Without a fix, the useful levers are exposure reductions such as removing the feature or restricting reach, both of which change how much can be exploited. Believing only a vendor build can help is the tempting error, and it leaves the depots exposed while waiting.
questions.hint: Reach and feature use can be changed without a new build.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The interval between disclosure and deployment
questions.learningObjective: Calculate exposure remaining after a mitigation is deployed inside the window
questions.stem: An advisory is published on Monday, the fixed build arrives ten days later, and a mitigation goes live four days after publication. How many exposure days remain after that mitigation?
questions.explanation: Exposure runs from publication on day zero to the arriving build on day ten, and the mitigation on day four leaves 10 minus 4, which is 6 exposure days still to run. options.text: Whether the weakness applies to the depots at all, because only present weaknesses need work
options.misconception: jumps to priority before confirming applicability

options.text: Which depot has the newest consoles, since newness usually means exposure
options.misconception: uses hardware age as a substitute for applicability

options.text: How many staff know about the advisory, since awareness drives the real risk
options.misconception: treats knowledge of the advisory as the measure of risk

options.text: Which depot has the longest routes, since long routes mean more hours of exposure
options.misconception: confuses service length with technical exposure

questions.stem: Rolling stock is split into three groups that share one weakness. Which grouping helps the planner decide where to act?

options.text: By what can reach each group, since outward paths make some groups far more exposed
options.misconception: groups by device type rather than by reach

options.text: By the age of the vehicles, since newer vehicles are generally less exposed
options.misconception: assumes newer hardware means safer exposure

options.text: By the depot that owns them, since ownership decides who can act on them
options.misconception: treats ownership as the measure of technical exposure

options.text: By fuel type, since vehicles on one fuel share a common weakness profile
options.misconception: groups on an attribute unrelated to reach

questions.topic: Rating against reach
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether two ratings are consistent with the reach evidence
questions.stem: A review rated one weakness medium and another high, though both are the same kind of flaw. Which reading best fits the notes?

options.text: The higher-rated weakness is reachable from a shorter path, which raises how easily it is used
options.misconception: assumes ratings differ because the flaws differ in kind

options.text: The higher-rated weakness was found later, and later findings always carry higher ratings
options.misconception: believes discovery order sets severity

options.text: The medium-rated weakness is harder to reach, and harder to reach should mean more severe
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between reach and severity

options.text: The ratings differ only because one flaw was given a longer written description
options.misconception: treats write-up length as the cause of a rating

questions.explanation: Ratings reflect how reachable and how damaging the weakness is, so a shorter route from outside pushes a rating higher even for the same kind of flaw. Reading a rating difference as a difference in flaw kind, or inverting the reach relationship, is the tempting error.

options.misconception: assumes identical hardware implies a hardware fault

options.text: In the operator training, since each terminal depends on what staff are taught
options.misconception: blames behaviour when a common setting explains it

options.text: In the timetable data, because every stop shares the same route file
options.misconception: treats shared data as the source of a security weakness

options.text: In the radio network, since all stops use one frequency for dispatch calls
options.misconception: attributes it to shared infrastructure without evidence

options.text: Turning off the feature that carries the weakness, so there is nothing left to exploit
options.misconception: equates reducing use with making the weakness harmless

options.text: Writing a note in the operations handbook that the feature should be used carefully
options.misconception: mistakes guidance for a technical reduction of exposure

options.text: Waiting for the supplier, because manual steps cannot alter exposure at all
options.misconception: believes only vendor changes alter exposure

options.text: Restoring a default that was changed years ago, since defaults are always safer
options.misconception: assumes a default is safer without checking its value

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the disclosure interval from the period of actual exposure
questions.stem: Even though the advisory names a fix that is already available, the depot has not deployed it for nine days. What does the planner report?

options.text: Nine days of continued exposure, because the fix being available is not the fix running
options.misconception: treats availability of a fix as deployment of a fix

options.text: No exposure, because a published fix protects every site automatically
options.misconception: believes a published fix protects sites with no action

options.text: Nine days of paperwork delay only, since the flaw is inert in the field
options.misconception: assumes a weakness is inert until someone exploits it

options.text: One day, because only the day of the report counts towards exposure
options.misconception: counts the report day instead of the whole delay

questions.explanation: Exposure continues until the remedy is actually running, so nine days of not deploying is nine days of exposure even though a fix exists. Confusing availability with deployment, or believing a flaw is inert until exploited, is the tempting error.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of handling a published weakness
questions.learningObjective: Justify the sequence of assessing, prioritising and remediating a weakness
questions.stem: Explain why the sequence for a published weakness should be check applicability, rank by exposure, mitigate, then deploy the permanent fix.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that each step answers a question the previous one cannot: applicability decides whether the weakness is real for this estate, ranking by exposure decides who is served first, mitigation protects the gap while the fix is built, and the permanent fix closes the weakness rather than narrowing it. It adds that skipping the mitigation leaves the ranked window fully open, and that ranking before applicability spends effort on flaws that do not apply here.

questions.explanation: The order is a chain of dependencies, since ranking and mitigation are only meaningful for weaknesses that actually apply to the depot. Assuming the ranking can come first, or that the permanent fix makes mitigation unnecessary, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Each step answers a question the previous one cannot.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of handling a published weakness
questions.learningObjective: Explain why mitigation precedes permanent remediation
questions.stem: Explain why a mitigation available today is applied before a permanent fix that takes six weeks to reach the fleet.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that the two actions protect for different lengths of time, so a mitigation available now shortens the period of live exposure while the permanent build is still six weeks away, whereas the permanent fix only reduces exposure once it is installed on the last vehicle. It notes that the mitigation is a reduction rather than a cure, so the permanent fix must still be scheduled and tracked, and that skipping the mitigation would leave the whole six week window fully exposed.

questions.explanation: A mitigation shortens the window of live exposure now, while the permanent fix only helps once it has reached the whole fleet. Believing a workaround can replace the permanent fix, or that mitigation is only paperwork, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: The point is to shorten the window of live exposure.

questions.learningObjective: Relate a slow deployment plan to the length of the exposure window
questions.stem: A fourth rollout plan updates 30 of 200 terminals each night, so it takes seven nights to finish. What does that do to exposure?

options.text: It stretches the window, because unpatched terminals stay exposed across several nights
options.misconception: believes a rollout shortens exposure as soon as it starts

options.text: It has no effect, because exposure depends only on the advisory's publication date
options.misconception: ties exposure to publication alone

options.text: It halves exposure immediately, because the first night patches thirty terminals
options.misconception: assumes partial patching removes the whole weakness

options.text: It creates a second weakness, since mixed builds confuse the monitoring
options.misconception: invents a new weakness from a staged rollout

questions.explanation: Exposure lasts until the last affected terminal is patched, so a seven-night rollout leaves unpatched terminals exposed for that whole period. Assuming exposure ends when the rollout starts, or halves with the first batch, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Exposure ends at the last patched terminal.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of handling a published weakness
questions.learningObjective: Run two stages from an applicability check to a chosen action
questions.stem: First decide which depots the weakness applies to, then pick the action. It needs a feature enabled on the depot build, and only the two city depots run that build.

options.text: It applies to the two city depots, so the permanent fix should be installed there first
options.misconception: starts the permanent fix without ranking or mitigation

options.text: It applies to every depot, so the same treatment should be applied across the network
options.misconception: assumes an advisory applies to every build in use

options.text: It applies to the two city depots, so effort goes to ranking and mitigating those first
options.misconception: reaches the right first step but then ignores it

options.text: It applies to no depot, so the advisory can be closed without any further work
options.misconception: reverses the applicability finding and closes the item

questions.explanation: Only the two city depots run a build with the feature, so the applicability check narrows the work to those two, and ranking plus mitigation is the right next step there. Treating the advisory as universal, or closing it outright, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Narrow by build, then rank and mitigate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Ranking groups by exposure rather than by count
questions.learningObjective: Rank weakness groups by exposure using a shared dataset

stimulus.body: The depot board has three candidate groups. A holds 120 weak terminals on a closed internal network. B holds 25 weak terminals reachable from the yard wireless. C holds 6 weak terminals that accept direct connections from the public link. The board must pick one group for this month.

questions.stem: Given that note, which group does the board pick for this month?

options.text: Group C, because those six terminals can be connected to directly from outside
options.misconception: picks the smallest group without weighing the outward path

options.text: Group A, because 120 weak terminals is by far the largest number affected
options.misconception: ranks by group size and ignores the path out

options.text: Group B, because twenty-five reachable terminals beat six public ones on volume
options.misconception: compares counts instead of reach

options.text: All three groups, because a monthly programme should cover the whole estate
options.misconception: assumes breadth is required when a choice was asked for

questions.explanation: Six terminals that accept direct public connections offer the widest path in, so they carry the most exposure per device and should lead the month. Ranking by group size, or treating breadth as the goal, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Pick the group with the widest path in.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Rating against reach
questions.learningObjective: Compare two weakness ratings using the reach evidence behind them
questions.stem: Another team rated a similar weakness lower because the affected kit sits behind a jump host. Explain whether that rating holds up.

answer.exemplar: A model answer argues that a jump host narrows the set of things able to connect directly to the kit, so the reach argument for the lower rating does hold, and that the rating is defensible because the path has been channelled rather than left open. It warns that the rating must still be revisited if the host is ever exposed to the same public link as the kit, because a channelled path and an open path are not the same thing and the whole judgement rests on that difference.

questions.explanation: A controlled hop in the path narrows who can connect, so a lower rating can be justified by it. Assuming a jump host removes the path rather than channelling it, and never needing review, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask whether the hop narrows or merely reroutes the path.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A default that widens reach
questions.learningObjective: Recall that a permissive default enlarges the set of devices that can reach a system
questions.stem: A council reviews four terminal settings and asks which one widens reach the most.

options.text: Remote clipboard sharing, because sharing content counts as sharing the session
options.misconception: assumes clipboard sharing opens the terminal to outsiders

options.text: The default guest account, because it lets any device on the wireless act on the terminal
options.misconception: treats a convenience setting as if it narrowed reach

options.text: Auto-update, because automatic updates reach out to the vendor on every check
options.misconception: treats outbound checks as inbound reach

options.text: The five-minute screen lock, because a short lock invites others to try again
options.misconception: believes a short lock weakens the terminal remotely

questions.explanation: A default guest account removes the need to authenticate, so every device on the shared wireless joins the set that can act on the terminal. Treating clipboard sharing or auto-update as the wider path is the tempting error, since those concern data and outbound traffic.
questions.hint: Ask which setting lets anyone connect without proving who they are.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness that lives in the settings
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a settings table and identify the entry that widens reach
questions.stem: A depot's terminal inventory shows: 25 terminals with guest access on, 40 with firmware checks off, 12 with verbose error pages, and 6 with all three. Which group is most exposed by the settings?

options.text: The 40 with firmware checks off, since that is the largest number of terminals
options.misconception: picks the largest count rather than the reachable path

options.text: The 6 with all three, since several weak settings on one terminal compound the reach
options.misconception: focuses on a small group and misses the wider guest access group

options.text: The 12 with verbose error pages, because they reveal the internal layout to anyone
options.misconception: confuses information disclosure with an open reach path

options.text: The 25 with guest access on, since it lets any device reach the terminal unchecked
options.misconception: ignores the compounded group and dismisses open access

questions.explanation: Guest access removes the need to prove identity, so every device that can route to those 25 terminals joins the reachable set. Prioritising the largest count of a weaker setting, or the smallest compounded group, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask which setting lets anyone connect unchecked.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A weakness with no fix to install
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a settings change can remove or reintroduce a weakness
questions.stem: Recently a fleet refresh reverted two terminals to their factory settings, and the weakness came back. What does that tell the planner?

options.text: The devices are faulty, since only faulty hardware reverts its own configuration
options.misconception: assumes a settings revert indicates a hardware fault

options.text: The weakness depends on a stored setting, so a reset restores the vulnerable configuration
options.misconception: believes a reset always makes a device more secure

options.text: The weakness was never fixed, only hidden, which means it was always present
options.misconception: concludes a permanent absence of any earlier fix

options.text: The refresh is irrelevant, since weakness cannot depend on configuration at all
options.misconception: denies that configuration can carry a weakness

questions.explanation: The weakness returned with the factory settings, which shows it lives in a stored configuration value rather than in patched code. Assuming a reset improves security, or that weakness cannot depend on configuration, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: The reset brought something back; find out what.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The interval between disclosure and deployment
questions.learningObjective: Advise on shortening the gap between disclosure and deployment
questions.stem: Currently the depot waits three weeks between a published advisory and any remedy. What should the board change to shorten that gap?

options.text: The handover between the triage desk and the field team, since that is where the wait sits
options.misconception: assumes the delay is one handover rather than three stages

options.text: The nightly patching window, since more terminal capacity means less waiting
options.misconception: fixes one stage and leaves triage and testing untouched

options.text: The testing step, so that builds are approved the same day they arrive
options.misconception: addresses one stage and assumes the others are quick

options.text: Nothing structural, since a three week wait is normal for every vendor
options.misconception: accepts the delay as inevitable and stops looking

questions.explanation: The three week wait is the sum of triage, testing and rollout queues, so the testing step is often where the build sits unused, and shortening it removes that part of the gap. Assuming the wait is one handover, or that one stage explains it all, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Split the wait into stages and time each one.
